claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Avila Cobos et al., 2018).

claims.claim: A limitation of most deconvolution algorithms is that they do not predict the proportion of cell types that are not present in the reference profiles.
claims.source: A limitation of most deconvolution algorithms is that they do not predict the proportion of cell types that are not present in the reference profiles (hereafter referred to as 'uncharacterized' cells).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the limitations of existing deconvolution algorithms.

claims.claim: In the context of tumor samples, uncharacterized cell populations include malignant cells whose molecular profiles differ not only from one cancer type to another but also from one patient to another even within the same tumor type.
claims.source: In the context of tumor samples, these uncharacterized cell populations include malignant cells whose molecular profiles differ not only from one cancer type to another but also from one patient to another even within the same tumor type (Corces et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Corces et al., 2018).

claims.claim: A few tools developed for bulk RNA-Seq data consider uncharacterized cells in their deconvolution framework by using cell-type specific markers not expressed in the uncharacterized cells.
claims.source: To address this limitation, a few tools developed for bulk RNA-Seq data consider uncharacterized cells in their deconvolution framework by using cell-type specific markers not expressed in the uncharacterized cells (Gosink et al., 2007; Clarke et al., 2010; Racle et al., 2017; Finotello et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Gosink et al., 2007; Clarke et al., 2010; Racle et al., 2017; Finotello et al., 2019).

claims.claim: EPIC simultaneously quantifies immune, stromal, vascular as well as uncharacterized cells from bulk tumor samples.
claims.source: These tools include EPIC (estimating the proportion of immune and cancer cells) which simultaneously quantifies immune, stromal, vascular as well as uncharacterized cells from bulk tumor samples (Racle et al., 2017; Racle and Gfeller, 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Racle et al., 2017; Racle and Gfeller, 2020).

claims.claim: Most deconvolution algorithms have been developed for transcriptomic data (RNA-Seq data).
claims.source: Most deconvolution algorithms have been developed for transcriptomic data (RNA-Seq data) (Gong and Szustakowski, 2013; Newman et al., 2015; Newman et al., 2019; Racle et al., 2017; Finotello et al., 2019; Jiménez-Sánchez et al., 2019; Monaco et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Gong and Szustakowski, 2013; Newman et al., 2015; Newman et al., 2019; Racle et al., 2017; Finotello et al., 2019; Jiménez-Sánchez et al., 2019; Monaco et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020a).

claims.claim: Deconvolution algorithms have been proposed for methylation data.
claims.source: More recently they have been proposed for other omics layers such as methylation (Aryee et al., 2014; Teschendorff et al., 2017; Teschendorff et al., 2020; Chakravarthy et al., 2018; Hicks and Irizarry, 2019; Rahmani et al., 2019; Arneson et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a; Salas et al., 2022), proteomics (Feng et al., 2023), or chromatin accessibility (Li et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Aryee et al., 2014; Teschendorff et al., 2017; Teschendorff et al., 2020; Chakravarthy et al., 2018; Hicks and Irizarry, 2019; Rahmani et al., 2019; Arneson et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a; Salas et al., 2022).

claims.claim: Deconvolution algorithms have been proposed for proteomics data.
claims.source: More recently they have been proposed for other omics layers such as methylation (Aryee et al., 2014; Teschendorff et al., 2017; Teschendorff et al., 2020; Chakravarthy et al., 2018; Hicks and Irizarry, 2019; Rahmani et al., 2019; Arneson et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a; Salas et al., 2022), proteomics (Feng et al., 2023), or chromatin accessibility (Li et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Feng et al., 2023).

claims.claim: Deconvolution algorithms have been proposed for chromatin accessibility data.
claims.source: More recently they have been proposed for other omics layers such as methylation (Aryee et al., 2014; Teschendorff et al., 2017; Teschendorff et al., 2020; Chakravarthy et al., 2018; Hicks and Irizarry, 2019; Rahmani et al., 2019; Arneson et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021a; Salas et al., 2022), proteomics (Feng et al., 2023), or chromatin accessibility (Li et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Li et al., 2020b).

claims.claim: DeconPeaker was developed to estimate cell-type proportions from bulk ATAC-Seq samples.
claims.source: For the latter, a specific framework called DeconPeaker (Li et al., 2020b) was developed to estimate cell-type proportions from bulk ATAC-Seq samples.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Li et al., 2020b).

claims.claim: Deconvolution tools developed initially for RNA-Seq data can be applied to ATAC-Seq.
claims.source: Deconvolution tools developed initially for RNA-Seq data can also be applied to ATAC-Seq.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent example of CIBERSORT being used with ATAC-Seq data.

claims.claim: CIBERSORT in combination with ATAC-Seq profiles was used to deconvolve leukemic ATAC-Seq samples.
claims.source: For example, the popular deconvolution tool, CIBERSORT (Newman et al., 2015), in combination with ATAC-Seq profiles, was used to deconvolve leukemic ATAC-Seq samples (Corces et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Newman et al., 2015; Corces et al., 2016).

claims.claim: The application of existing bulk ATAC-Seq data deconvolution tools to solid tumors faces some limitations.
claims.source: The application of existing bulk ATAC-Seq data deconvolution tools to solid tumors faces some limitations.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of the field, which is then elaborated upon.

claims.claim: Current computational frameworks do not quantify populations of uncharacterized cell types.
claims.source: First, current computational frameworks do not quantify populations of uncharacterized cell types.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on the authors' knowledge of existing deconvolution frameworks for ATAC-Seq data.

claims.claim: ATAC-Seq-based markers and reference profiles generated so far have been derived in the context of hematopoietic cell mixtures.
claims.source: Second, ATAC-Seq-based markers (i.e. chromatin-accessible regions called peaks) and reference profiles generated so far have been derived in the context of hematopoietic cell mixtures (Corces et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020b).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Corces et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020b).

claims.claim: Markers and profiles for major populations of the TME (e.g. stromal and vascular cells) are missing from existing ATAC-Seq deconvolution tools.
claims.source: Markers and profiles for major populations of the TME (e.g. stromal and vascular cells) are thus missing.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of the field, following from the previous statement about hematopoietic cell mixtures.

claims.claim: Cell-type specific markers have been identified from scATAC-Seq data.
claims.source: While cell-type specific markers have been identified from scATAC-Seq data (Zhang et al., 2021b), not all TME-relevant cell types are covered (e.g. lack of scATAC-Seq data from neutrophils due to extracellular traps formation).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Zhang et al., 2021b).

claims.claim: Not all TME-relevant cell types are covered by cell-type specific markers identified from scATAC-Seq data.
claims.source: While cell-type specific markers have been identified from scATAC-Seq data (Zhang et al., 2021b), not all TME-relevant cell types are covered (e.g. lack of scATAC-Seq data from neutrophils due to extracellular traps formation).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by the example of neutrophils and the citation to prior research (Zhang et al., 2021b).

claims.claim: There is a lack of scATAC-Seq data from neutrophils due to extracellular traps formation.
claims.source: While cell-type specific markers have been identified from scATAC-Seq data (Zhang et al., 2021b), not all TME-relevant cell types are covered (e.g. lack of scATAC-Seq data from neutrophils due to extracellular traps formation).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the technical challenges of performing scATAC-Seq on neutrophils.

claims.claim: Many cell-type specific markers from scATAC-Seq data have not been curated to fulfill the requirements of tools such as EPIC to quantify uncharacterized cells.
claims.source: Many of these markers have also not been curated to fulfill the requirements of tools such as EPIC to quantify uncharacterized cells (i.e. markers of a cell type should not be accessible in other human tissues).
claims.evidence: This statement is based on the authors' assessment of existing markers and the requirements of the EPIC framework.

claims.claim: The authors collected ATAC-Seq data from pure cell types to identify cell-type specific marker peaks and to build reference profiles from most major non-malignant cell types typically observed in tumors.
claims.source: In this study, we collected ATAC-Seq data from pure cell types to identify cell-type specific marker peaks and to build reference profiles from most major non-malignant cell types typically observed in tumors.
claims.evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented.

claims.claim: The authors integrated ATAC-Seq data into the EPIC framework to perform bulk ATAC-Seq samples deconvolution.
claims.source: These data were integrated into the EPIC (Racle et al., 2017) framework to perform bulk ATAC-Seq samples deconvolution (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data and Figure 1.

claims.claim: Applied on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and tumor samples, the EPIC-ATAC framework showed accurate predictions of the proportions of non-malignant and malignant cells.
claims.source: Applied on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and tumor samples, the EPIC-ATAC framework showed accurate predictions of the proportions of non-malignant and malignant cells.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the benchmarking data presented in the results section.

claims.claim: 564 pure ATAC-Seq data of sorted cells were collected to build reference profiles for non-malignant cell types observed in the tumor microenvironment.
claims.source: (1) 564 pure ATAC-Seq data of sorted cells were collected to build reference profiles for non-malignant cell types observed in the tumor microenvironment.
claims.evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented and Figure 1.

claims.claim: Cell-type specific marker peaks were identified using differential accessibility analysis.
claims.source: (2) Cell-type specific marker peaks were identified using differential accessibility analysis.
claims.evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented and Figure 1.

claims.claim: Markers with previously observed chromatin accessibility in human healthy tissues were excluded.
claims.source: (3) Markers with previously observed chromatin accessibility in human healthy tissues were excluded.
claims.evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented and Figure 1.

claims.claim: For tumor bulk deconvolution, the set of remaining marker peaks was refined by selecting markers with correlated behavior in tumor bulk samples.
claims.source: (4) For tumor bulk deconvolution, the set of remaining marker peaks was refined by selecting markers with correlated behavior in tumor bulk samples.
claims.evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented and Figure 1.

claims.claim: The cell-type specific marker peaks and reference profiles were integrated into the EPIC-ATAC framework to perform bulk ATAC-Seq deconvolution.
claims.source: (5) The cell-type specific marker peaks and reference profiles were integrated into the EPIC-ATAC framework to perform bulk ATAC-Seq deconvolution.
claims.evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented and Figure 1.

claims.claim: The authors collected 564 samples of sorted cell populations from twelve studies including B cells, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, monocytes, neutrophils, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells.
claims.source: To identify robust chromatin accessibility marker peaks of cell types observed in the tumor microenvironment, we collected 564 samples of sorted cell populations from twelve studies including B cells (Corces et al., 2016; Calderon et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022a), CD4+ T cells (Corces et al., 2016; Mumbach et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020; Giles et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022a), CD8+ T cells (Corces et al., 2016; Calderon et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020; Giles et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022a), natural killer (NK) cells (Corces et al., 2016; Calderon et al., 2019), dendritic cells (DCs) (mDCs and pDCs are grouped in this cell-type category) (Calderon et al., 2019; Leylek et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020), macrophages (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022a), monocytes (Corces et al., 2016; Calderon et al., 2019; Leylek et al., 2020; Trizzino et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022a), neutrophils (Perez et al., 2020; Ram-Mohan et al., 2021), fibroblasts (Liu et al., 2020; Ge et al., 2021), and endothelial cells (Liu et al., 2020; Xin et al., 2020; Figure 1 box 1, Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by the data presented, Figure 1, Figure 2A, and Supplementary file 1. The citations provide additional support.

claims.claim: To limit batch effects, the collected samples were homogeneously processed from read alignment to peak calling.
claims.source: To limit batch effects, the collected samples were homogeneously processed from read alignment to peak calling.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the data processing approach used in the study.

claims.claim: For each cell type, a set of stable peaks observed across samples and studies was derived.
claims.source: For each cell type, we derived a set of stable peaks observed across samples and studies, that is for each study, peaks detected in at least half of the samples were considered, and for each cell type, only peaks detected jointly in all studies were kept (see Materials and methods, 'Generation of an ATAC-Seq reference dataset of non-malignant cell types frequently observed in the tumor microenvironment').
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the peak selection approach used in the study.

claims.claim: Pairwise differential analysis was performed to identify marker peaks for each cell type.
claims.source: These peaks were then used to perform pairwise differential analysis to identify marker peaks for each cell type (Figure 1, Box 2).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak identification approach used in the study, supported by Figure 1.

claims.claim: To ensure that the cell-type specific marker peaks are not accessible in other human tissues, ATAC-Seq samples from diverse human tissues from the ENCODE data were included in the differential analysis.
claims.source: To ensure that the cell-type specific marker peaks are not accessible in other human tissues, we included in the differential analysis ATAC-Seq samples from diverse human tissues from the ENCODE data (Abascal et al., 2020; Rozowsky et al., 2023; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak identification approach used in the study, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claims.claim: The top 200 peaks recurrently differentially accessible across all cell-type pairs were selected as cell-type specific markers.
claims.source: To select a sufficient number of peaks prior to peak filtering, the top 200 peaks recurrently differentially accessible across all cell-type pairs were selected as cell-type specific markers (see Materials and methods, 'Identification of cell-type specific markers').
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak selection approach used in the study.

claims.claim: Markers overlapping modules of open chromatin regions accessible in human tissues from the human atlas study were excluded from the marker list.
claims.source: To filter out markers that could be accessible in other human cell types than those included in our reference profiles, we used the human atlas study (Zhang et al., 2021b), which identified modules of open chromatin regions accessible in a comprehensive set of human tissues, and we excluded from our marker list the markers overlapping these modules (Figure 1, box 3, see Materials and methods 'Identification of cell-type specific markers').
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak filtering approach used in the study, supported by Figure 1 and a citation.

claims.claim: The resulting marker peaks specific only to the immune cell types were considered for the deconvolution of PBMC samples (PBMC markers).
claims.source: The resulting marker peaks specific only to the immune cell types were considered for the deconvolution of PBMC samples (PBMC markers).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak selection for PBMC deconvolution.

claims.claim: For the deconvolution of tumor bulk samples, the lists of marker peaks specific to fibroblasts and endothelial cells were added to the PBMC markers.
claims.source: For the deconvolution of tumor bulk samples, the lists of marker peaks specific to fibroblasts and endothelial cells were added to the PBMC markers.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak selection for tumor bulk deconvolution.

claims.claim: The extended set of markers for tumor bulk deconvolution was further refined based on the correlation patterns of the markers in tumor bulk samples from diverse solid cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA).
claims.source: This extended set of markers was further refined based on the correlation patterns of the markers in tumor bulk samples from the diverse solid cancer types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA; https://www.cancergenomicscloud.org/datasets; Corces et al., 2018), that is markers exhibiting the highest correlation patterns in the tumor bulk samples were selected using the findCorrelation function from the caret R package (Kuhn, 2008; Figure 1, box 4, see the Materials and methods, 'Identification of cell-type specific markers').
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak refinement approach used in the study, supported by Figure 1 and citations.

claims.claim: A total of 716 markers of immune, fibroblasts, and endothelial cell types remained after the last filtering (defined as TME markers).
claims.source: A total of 716 markers of immune, fibroblasts, and endothelial cell types remained after the last filtering (defined as TME markers).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data processing and filtering steps described.

claims.claim: The authors recommend using the TME markers and profiles to deconvolve bulk samples from tumor samples and the PBMC markers and profiles to deconvolve PBMC samples.
claims.source: Considering the difference in cell types and the different filtering steps applied on the PBMC and TME markers, we recommend using the TME markers and profiles to deconvolve bulk samples from tumor samples and the PBMC markers and profiles to deconvolve PBMC samples.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the methodological differences between the PBMC and TME marker sets.

claims.claim: Principal component analysis based on each set of marker peaks showed that samples clustered by cell type and not by study of origin.
claims.source: To assess the quality and reproducibility of these markers, we first performed principal component analysis (PCA) based on each set of marker peaks. Computing silhouette coefficients based on the cell-type classification and on the study of origin showed that samples clustered by cell type and not by study of origin (averaged silhouette coefficients above 0.45 for cell type and around 0 for the study of origin).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the PCA analysis and silhouette coefficient calculations.

claims.claim: Averaged silhouette coefficients were above 0.45 for cell type and around 0 for the study of origin.
claims.source: Computing silhouette coefficients based on the cell-type classification and on the study of origin showed that samples clustered by cell type and not by study of origin (averaged silhouette coefficients above 0.45 for cell type and around 0 for the study of origin).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the silhouette coefficient calculations.

claims.claim: The representation of the samples based on the first axes of the PCA confirmed that samples clustered by cell type and not by study of origin.
claims.source: The representation of the samples based on the first axes of the PCA confirmed this observation (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The results indicate limited remaining batch effects after data processing and marker selection.
claims.source: These results indicate limited remaining batch effects after data processing and marker selection.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA and silhouette coefficient results.

claims.claim: The collected samples were used to generate chromatin accessibility profiles by computing the average of the normalized counts for each peak in each cell type as well as peak variability in each cell type.
claims.source: We then used the collected samples to generate chromatin accessibility profiles by computing the average of the normalized counts for each peak in each cell type as well as peak variability in each cell type (see Materials and methods) since EPIC uses features variability for the estimation of the cell-type proportions (Racle et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the reference profile generation approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Figure 2C represents the average chromatin accessibility of each marker peak in each cell type of the reference dataset and highlights the cell-type specificity of the selected markers.
claims.source: Figure 2C represents the average chromatin accessibility of each marker peak in each cell type of the reference dataset and highlights, as expected, the cell-type specificity of the selected markers (see also Supplementary files 2 and 3), which was confirmed in independent ATAC-Seq data from sorted cells and single-cell ATAC-Seq samples from blood and diverse human tissues (Figure 2D and E, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 2C, Figure 2D, Figure 2E, and Supplementary files 2 and 3.

claims.claim: The cell-type specificity of the selected markers was confirmed in independent ATAC-Seq data from sorted cells and single-cell ATAC-Seq samples from blood and diverse human tissues.
claims.source: Figure 2C represents the average chromatin accessibility of each marker peak in each cell type of the reference dataset and highlights, as expected, the cell-type specificity of the selected markers (see also Supplementary files 2 and 3), which was confirmed in independent ATAC-Seq data from sorted cells and single-cell ATAC-Seq samples from blood and diverse human tissues (Figure 2D and E, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 2D and Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Most of the markers are in distal and intergenic regions.
claims.source: We observed that most of the markers are in distal and intergenic regions (Figure 2F), which is expected considering the large proportion of distal regions in the human genome and the fact that such regions have been previously described as highly cell-type specific (Corces et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 2F and a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Distal regions have been previously described as highly cell-type specific.
claims.source: We observed that most of the markers are in distal and intergenic regions (Figure 2F), which is expected considering the large proportion of distal regions in the human genome and the fact that such regions have been previously described as highly cell-type specific (Corces et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research (Corces et al., 2016).

claims.claim: 7% of the PBMC and TME marker peaks are in promoter regions in contrast to 4% when considering matched genomic regions randomly selected in the set of peaks identified prior to the differential analysis.
claims.source: We also noticed that 7% of the PBMC and TME marker peaks are in promoter regions in contrast to 4% when considering matched genomic regions randomly selected in the set of peaks identified prior to the differential analysis (see Materials and methods), which suggests enrichment in our marker peaks for important regulatory regions.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the annotation analysis.

claims.claim: The observation that 7% of the PBMC and TME marker peaks are in promoter regions suggests enrichment in marker peaks for important regulatory regions.
claims.source: We also noticed that 7% of the PBMC and TME marker peaks are in promoter regions in contrast to 4% when considering matched genomic regions randomly selected in the set of peaks identified prior to the differential analysis (see Materials and methods), which suggests enrichment in our marker peaks for important regulatory regions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of promoter region percentages.

claims.claim: Each marker peak was associated with its nearest gene using ChIP-Enrich based on the 'nearest transcription start site (TSS)' locus definition.
claims.source: To assess the biological relevance of the marker peaks, we associated each marker peak with its nearest gene using ChIP-Enrich based on the 'nearest transcription start site (TSS)' locus definition (Welch et al., 2014; Supplementary files 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the marker peak annotation approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In each set of cell-type specific peaks, there was an overrepresentation of chromatin binding proteins (CBPs) reported in the JASPAR2022 database.
claims.source: In each set of cell-type specific peaks, we observed an overrepresentation of chromatin binding proteins (CBPs) reported in the JASPAR2022 database (Castro-Mondragon et al., 2022) (using Signac Stuart et al., 2021 and MonaLisa Machlab et al., 2022 for assessing the overrepresentation) and the ReMap catalog (Hammal et al., 2022) (using RemapEnrich, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the enrichment analysis and citations.

claims.claim: In each set of cell-type specific peaks, there was an overrepresentation of chromatin binding proteins (CBPs) reported in the ReMap catalog.
claims.source: In each set of cell-type specific peaks, we observed an overrepresentation of chromatin binding proteins (CBPs) reported in the JASPAR2022 database (Castro-Mondragon et al., 2022) (using Signac Stuart et al., 2021 and MonaLisa Machlab et al., 2022 for assessing the overrepresentation) and the ReMap catalog (Hammal et al., 2022) (using RemapEnrich, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the enrichment analysis and citations.

claims.claim: Based on the 'nearest TSS' annotation, each set of cell-type specific marker peaks was tested for enrichment in regions linked to specific biological pathways (GO pathways) using ChIP-Enrich.
claims.source: Based on the 'nearest TSS' annotation, we tested, using ChIP-Enrich (Welch et al., 2014), whether each set of cell-type specific marker peaks was enriched for regions linked to specific biological pathways (GO pathways).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the pathway enrichment analysis approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Figure 2G highlights a subset of the enriched pathways that are consistent with prior knowledge of each cell type.
claims.source: Figure 2G highlights a subset of the enriched pathways that are consistent with prior knowledge of each cell type.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Some of the enriched pathways are known to be characteristic of immune responses to inflammatory or tumoral environments.
claims.source: Some of these pathways are known to be characteristic of immune responses to inflammatory or tumoral environments.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on knowledge about the biological functions of the enriched pathways.

claims.claim: The analyses demonstrate that the proposed cell-type specific marker peaks capture some of the known biological properties associated with each cell type.
claims.source: Overall, these analyses demonstrate that the proposed cell-type specific marker peaks capture some of the known biological properties associated with each cell type.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the annotation and enrichment analyses.

claims.claim: The cell-type specific marker peaks and profiles derived from the reference samples were integrated into the EPIC deconvolution tool.
claims.source: The cell-type specific marker peaks and profiles derived from the reference samples were integrated into the EPIC deconvolution tool (Racle et al., 2017; Racle and Gfeller, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a primary methodological contribution of the study, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The ATAC-Seq deconvolution framework is referred to as EPIC-ATAC.
claims.source: We will refer to this ATAC-Seq deconvolution framework as EPIC-ATAC.
claims.evidence: This is a naming convention established by the authors.

claims.claim: An option is provided to lift over hg19 datasets to hg38 to ensure the compatibility of any input bulk ATAC-Seq dataset with the EPIC-ATAC marker peaks and reference profiles.
claims.source: To ensure the compatibility of any input bulk ATAC-Seq dataset with the EPIC-ATAC marker peaks and reference profiles, we provide an option to lift over hg19 datasets to hg38 (using the liftOver R package) as the reference profiles are based on the hg38 reference genome.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claims.claim: The reference profiles are based on the hg38 reference genome.
claims.source: To ensure the compatibility of any input bulk ATAC-Seq dataset with the EPIC-ATAC marker peaks and reference profiles, we provide an option to lift over hg19 datasets to hg38 (using the liftOver R package) as the reference profiles are based on the hg38 reference genome.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claims.claim: The features of the input bulk matrix are matched to the reference profiles' features.
claims.source: Subsequently, the features of the input bulk matrix are matched to our reference profiles' features.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claims.claim: To match both sets of features, the distance to the nearest peak in the reference profiles peaks is determined for each peak of the input bulk matrix.
claims.source: To match both sets of features, we determine for each peak of the input bulk matrix the distance to the nearest peak in the reference profiles peaks.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claims.claim: Overlapping regions are retained and the feature IDs are matched to their associated nearest peaks.
claims.source: Overlapping regions are retained and the feature IDs are matched to their associated nearest peaks.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claims.claim: If multiple features are matched to the same reference peak, the counts are summed.
claims.source: If multiple features are matched to the same reference peak, the counts are summed.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework.

claims.claim: Before the estimation of the cell-type proportions, the data are transformed following an approach similar to the transcripts per million (TPM) transformation.
claims.source: Before the estimation of the cell-type proportions, we transform the data following an approach similar to the transcripts per million (TPM) transformation which has been shown to be appropriate for estimating cell fractions from bulk mixtures in RNA-Seq data (Racle et al., 2017; Sturm et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the EPIC-ATAC framework, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The TPM transformation has been shown to be appropriate for estimating cell fractions from bulk mixtures in RNA-Seq data.
claims.source: Before the estimation of the cell-type proportions, we transform the data following an approach similar to the transcripts per million (TPM) transformation which has been shown to be appropriate for estimating cell fractions from bulk mixtures in RNA-Seq data (Racle et al., 2017; Sturm et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Racle et al., 2017; Sturm et al., 2019).

claims.claim: ATAC-Seq counts are normalized by dividing counts by the peak lengths as well as sample depth and rescaling counts so that the counts of each sample sum to 10^6.
claims.source: We normalize the ATAC-Seq counts by dividing counts by the peak lengths as well as sample depth and rescaling counts so that the counts of each sample sum to 106.

results.result: The authors collected 564 ATAC-Seq samples from sorted cell populations across 12 studies, covering 10 major cell types (B cells, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, NK cells, dendritic cells, macrophages, monocytes, neutrophils, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells) frequently observed in the tumor microenvironment. These samples were homogeneously processed to limit batch effects, and stable peaks observed across samples and studies were derived for each cell type to build reference profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C46, C49, C54, C179, and C180 are directly supported by the data collection and processing methodology described in the manuscript. The collection of 564 samples from 12 studies (C54) with homogeneous processing (C55) and derivation of stable peaks (C56) provides a solid foundation for the reference profiles. Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1 provide supporting evidence.

results.result: Cell-type specific marker peaks were identified through pairwise differential accessibility analysis, including ENCODE tissue samples to ensure markers were not accessible in other human tissues. After filtering using the human atlas study to exclude markers accessible in other tissues, 716 TME markers remained for tumor deconvolution and a separate set of PBMC markers was created for PBMC sample deconvolution.
results.evaluation: The marker peak identification methodology is well-documented across claims C50-C64. The differential analysis approach (C57), inclusion of ENCODE samples (C58), filtering using the human atlas (C60), and refinement based on TCGA correlation patterns (C63) represent a rigorous multi-step process. The final count of 716 TME markers (C64) is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 1.

results.result: Principal component analysis based on marker peaks showed that samples clustered by cell type rather than study of origin, with averaged silhouette coefficients above 0.45 for cell type and around 0 for study of origin, indicating limited remaining batch effects after data processing and marker selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by the PCA analysis results. The silhouette coefficient values (C67) provide quantitative evidence for clustering by cell type, and Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 provide visual confirmation (C68). The inference about limited batch effects (C69) is reasonable given the quantitative metrics.

results.result: The selected marker peaks demonstrated cell-type specificity in the reference dataset and were validated in independent ATAC-Seq data from sorted cells and single-cell ATAC-Seq samples. Most markers were located in distal and intergenic regions, with 7% in promoter regions compared to 4% in randomly selected peaks, suggesting enrichment for important regulatory regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 are supported by multiple lines of evidence. Figure 2C shows cell-type specificity in the reference dataset, while Figure 2D and 2E confirm this in independent data (C72). The genomic location analysis (C73, C75) is supported by Figure 2F, and the inference about regulatory region enrichment (C76) is reasonable based on the promoter enrichment comparison.

results.result: Marker peaks were annotated using ChIP-Enrich to identify nearest genes and tested for enrichment of chromatin binding proteins (CBPs) from JASPAR2022 and ReMap databases, as well as enrichment in biological pathways. The analyses demonstrated that the marker peaks capture known biological properties associated with each cell type.
results.evaluation: The annotation analyses (C77-C81) are methodologically sound and supported by the data. The use of multiple databases (JASPAR2022, ReMap) and enrichment analysis tools provides robust evidence. Figure 2G and Table 1 support the findings. The conclusion that marker peaks capture known biological properties (C83) is a reasonable inference from the enrichment results.

results.result: The cell-type specific marker peaks and reference profiles were integrated into the EPIC deconvolution framework, creating EPIC-ATAC. The framework includes options for genome build compatibility (hg19 to hg38 liftover), feature matching between input data and reference profiles, and TPM-like normalization of ATAC-Seq counts before cell-type proportion estimation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C47, C53, C84-C96 describe the methodological integration of the marker peaks and profiles into EPIC. The framework is well-documented with clear steps for data processing, normalization, and deconvolution. The TPM-like transformation (C92, C94) is justified by citations to prior work (C93). The methodological choices are appropriate for ATAC-Seq data.

results.result: EPIC-ATAC was validated on bulk ATAC-Seq data from five healthy donor PBMCs with matched flow cytometry data, showing predicted cell fractions consistent with flow cytometry measurements (Pearson correlation 0.78, RMSE 0.10). However, accuracy varied across samples, with one outlier sample (Sample4) showing larger discrepancies, possibly due to unusually high ATAC-Seq accessibility at monocyte and dendritic cell marker peaks.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C48, C98-C105 are supported by the experimental validation. The correlation and RMSE values (C101) provide quantitative evidence of accuracy. The identification of Sample4 as an outlier (C103) and the proposed explanation based on marker peak accessibility (C104, C105) are supported by Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The acknowledgment of variable accuracy (C102) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: EPIC-ATAC was validated on pseudobulk PBMC samples generated from three publicly available scATAC-Seq datasets, showing high correlation (0.91) and low RMSE (0.05) between predictions and true cell-type proportions.
results.evaluation: Claims C106 and C107 are supported by the pseudobulk validation results. The high correlation and low RMSE values are explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3C. The use of multiple independent scATAC-Seq datasets strengthens the validation.

results.result: EPIC-ATAC was benchmarked against other deconvolution tools (DeconPeaker, CIBERSORTx, quanTIseq, ABIS, MCPcounter) using the same reference profiles and marker peaks. Many tools displayed high correlation and low RMSE values similar to EPIC-ATAC, with no single tool consistently outperforming others, demonstrating the broad applicability of the curated marker peaks and reference profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C115 are supported by the benchmarking analysis. The comparison methodology (C108-C110) is appropriate, and the results (C114) are supported by Figure 3D-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The inference about broad applicability (C115) is reasonable given that multiple tools performed well with the same reference data.

results.result: EPIC-ATAC was evaluated on cancer pseudobulk samples from basal cell carcinoma, gynecological cancer, and HTAN datasets, demonstrating the ability to simultaneously predict proportions of both uncharacterized cells (serving as a proxy for cancer cells in most cases) and immune, stromal, and vascular cells across most cancer types.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C123 are supported by the cancer sample validation. The methodology (C117, C118) is appropriate, and the results (C119, C123) are supported by Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The interpretation that uncharacterized cells serve as a proxy for cancer cells (C120) is reasonable, with appropriate caveats for the HTAN dataset (C121, C122).

results.result: In benchmarking on cancer datasets, EPIC-ATAC achieved the highest performance and was the only method to accurately predict uncharacterized cell proportions. When excluding uncharacterized cells from the evaluation, EPIC-ATAC still outperformed most other methods. The advantage of EPIC-ATAC and quanTIseq in predicting absolute cell-type fractions (including uncharacterized cells) was significant compared to tools that only predict relative fractions.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C133 are supported by the benchmarking results on cancer datasets. The superior performance of EPIC-ATAC (C125) is documented in Figure 4B and related supplements. The comparison with quanTIseq (C126) and the two-benchmark approach (C132, C133) demonstrate rigorous evaluation. The distinction between absolute and relative fractions (C127-C129) is an important methodological consideration.

results.result: Cell-type-specific evaluation of EPIC-ATAC predictions revealed that NK cells, endothelial cells, neutrophils, and dendritic cells showed lower correlation values, explained by their low abundance in benchmarking datasets. For endothelial and dendritic cells, low RMSE values suggest reliable within-sample quantification despite lower between-sample precision. NK cells and neutrophils showed higher variability, suggesting potential for improvement in their markers and profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C141 are supported by the cell-type-specific analysis. The observation of lower correlations for certain cell types (C136) and the explanation based on abundance (C137) are supported by Figure 5A. The distinction between endothelial/dendritic cells (C138, C139) and NK/neutrophils (C140) based on RMSE values is appropriate. The comparison with other tools (C141) is supported by Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

results.result: EPIC-ATAC was evaluated for predicting T-cell subtype proportions (naive and non-naive CD8+, naive, helper/memory, and regulatory CD4+ T cells). Correlations between predictions and true proportions decreased when considering T-cell subtypes compared to major CD4+ and CD8+ populations, with particularly low accuracies for helper/memory CD4+ and naive T-cell subtypes. Similar results were obtained with other deconvolution tools.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C149 are supported by the T-cell subtype analysis. The methodology (C142-C144) is appropriate, and the validation of markers in external data (C145) is documented in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B. The decreased performance for subtypes (C147, C148) is supported by Figure 5B-C, and the comparison with other tools (C149) is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4. This represents an honest assessment of the method's limitations for closely related cell types.

results.result: EPIC-ATAC was applied to a breast cancer cohort of 42 samples (35 ER+/HER2- and 7 TNBC), showing high correlation (0.5-0.94) with the original study's cell-type infiltration metric. EPIC-ATAC identified higher proportions of T, B, and NK cells in TNBC versus ER+/HER2- samples, and differences in cellular composition among ER+/HER2- subgroups (CA-A, CA-B, CA-C), largely recapitulating findings from the original study with some differences in myeloid cell quantification.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C150-C162 are supported by the breast cancer cohort analysis. The high correlation with the original study's metric (C155) is documented in Figure 6A. The differences between breast cancer subtypes (C156) and subgroups (C158, C159) are supported by Figure 6B-C. The comparison with the original study (C160) and the additional findings for macrophages (C161) and NK cells (C162) demonstrate both validation and novel insights. This represents a successful real-world application of EPIC-ATAC.

results.result: Comparison of EPIC-ATAC (on ATAC-Seq data) with EPIC-RNA (on RNA-Seq data) using single-cell multiomic data from 10x PBMC and HTAN datasets showed that EPIC-ATAC performs similarly to EPIC RNA-seq-based deconvolution and outperforms gene activity (GA)-based RNA deconvolution. The lower performance of GA-based deconvolution was attributed to imperfect matching between GA features and transcriptomic data.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C171 are supported by the modality comparison analysis. The methodology using multiomic data (C164, C165) is appropriate for direct comparison. The results (C170) are supported by Figure 7A-B. The explanation for GA-based deconvolution's lower performance (C171) is a reasonable inference. This comparison provides important context for understanding EPIC-ATAC's performance relative to established RNA-seq methods.

results.result: On bulk PBMC samples with matched ATAC-Seq, RNA-Seq, and flow cytometry data, EPIC-ATAC predictions were better correlated with flow cytometry for some cell types (CD8+, CD4+ T cells, NK cells) while EPIC-RNA predictions were better for others (B cells, neutrophils, monocytes). Averaging predictions from both modalities showed moderate improvement, suggesting the two modalities can complement each other.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C178 are supported by the matched bulk data analysis. The cell-type-specific performance differences (C174, C175) are documented in Figure 7C. The moderate improvement from averaging (C177) and the inference about complementarity (C178) are supported by the data. This represents an important finding about the potential for multi-modal deconvolution approaches.

results.result: EPIC-ATAC framework allows accurate prediction of uncharacterized cell proportions (cells not included in reference profiles), which approximates the proportion of cancer cells in most cases since major TME cell types are included in the reference profiles.
results.evaluation: Claims C186 and C188 are supported by the cancer dataset validation results shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The ability to predict uncharacterized cells is a key distinguishing feature of EPIC-ATAC compared to other tools (C125). The inference that uncharacterized cells approximate cancer cells (C188) is reasonable given the comprehensive coverage of TME cell types in the reference profiles, though appropriate caveats are noted (C187).

results.result: The evaluation of EPIC-ATAC deconvolution resulted in an average absolute error of 8% across cell types, consistent with previous observations in RNA-Seq data deconvolution. Given this uncertainty, quantification of low-frequency populations remains challenging, and comparisons of such estimations across samples should be performed with care.
results.evaluation: Claims C199-C202 provide an honest assessment of EPIC-ATAC's accuracy and limitations. The 8% average error (C199) is explicitly stated and consistent with prior RNA-Seq deconvolution work (C200, supported by citation to Racle et al., 2017). The acknowledgment of challenges with low-frequency populations (C201, C202) is supported by citation to Jin and Liu, 2021 and by Figure 5A. This represents appropriate scientific caution about the method's limitations.

results.result: Cell-type deconvolution reaches a limitation when closely related cell types are considered. In this study, this limit was reached when considering T-cell subtypes in the reference profiles. The authors recommend using EPIC-ATAC with markers and reference profiles based on major cell-type populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C203-C205 are supported by the T-cell subtype analysis results (Figure 5B-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 4). The acknowledgment of this limitation (C203, C204) is based on empirical evidence showing decreased performance for T-cell subtypes. The recommendation to use major cell-type populations (C205) is a reasonable inference from these results. This represents honest reporting of method limitations.

results.result: Comparison of EPIC-ATAC applied on ATAC-Seq data with EPIC applied on RNA-Seq data showed that both modalities led to similar performances and could complement each other.
results.evaluation: Claim C208 is supported by the modality comparison results shown in Figure 7. Both the pseudobulk analysis (Figure 7A-B) and the bulk PBMC analysis (Figure 7C) demonstrate similar performance between ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq based deconvolution, with evidence of complementarity when predictions are combined (C177, C178).

results.result: The authors identified biologically relevant cell-type specific chromatin accessibility markers and profiles for most non-malignant cell types in the tumor microenvironment, capitalized on these to predict cell-type proportions from bulk PBMC and tumor ATAC-Seq data, and demonstrated reliable predictions of immune, stromal, vascular, and cancer cell proportions across diverse tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C220-C222 summarize the main contributions of the study. The identification of markers and profiles (C220) is supported by the data collection and analysis (C3, C46, C54, C71-C83). The prediction of cell-type proportions (C221) is supported by the EPIC-ATAC framework development (C4, C47, C84-C96). The demonstration of reliable predictions (C222) is supported by multiple validation analyses (C101, C107, C119, C155). These claims represent an accurate summary of the study's major findings.

results.result: The authors developed EPIC-ATAC by collecting 564 ATAC-Seq samples from 12 studies covering 10 cell types, identifying cell-type specific marker peaks through differential accessibility analysis, filtering markers accessible in other human tissues, refining markers based on correlation in tumor bulk samples, and integrating these into the EPIC deconvolution framework. This resulted in 716 TME markers and reference profiles for immune, stromal, and vascular cells.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the quality and rigor of the methodology. Reviewer 1 states the tool is 'timely' with 'rigorous methodologies,' Reviewer 2 describes the work as 'very high quality' with 'robust estimates,' and Reviewer 3 notes the authors have been 'incredibly thorough with their reference dataset collections.' No concerns are raised about the marker identification or reference profile generation process.

results.result: The marker peaks showed cell-type specificity with samples clustering by cell type rather than study of origin (silhouette coefficients >0.45 for cell type, ~0 for study), indicating limited batch effects. The markers were validated in independent data, enriched in distal/intergenic regions and promoters, and showed overrepresentation of relevant chromatin binding proteins and biological pathways consistent with each cell type's known functions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the characterization and validation of markers without critique. Reviewer 2 specifically praises the 'rigorous methodologies' and notes the 'newly-generated, validation data' are 'publicly available and well-documented.' The biological relevance and quality assessment of markers are implicitly accepted through the overall positive evaluation of the work.

results.result: EPIC-ATAC was validated on PBMC samples from five healthy donors with matched flow cytometry (correlation 0.78, RMSE 0.10) and on pseudobulk PBMC samples from scATAC-Seq data (correlation 0.91, RMSE 0.05). One outlier sample (Sample4) showed larger discrepancies, potentially due to unusually high accessibility at monocyte/dendritic markers.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the validation results. Reviewer 1 states the 'methodology and its application results on breast cancer tumor tissues are convincing,' Reviewer 2 notes the tool 'results in robust estimates,' and Reviewer 3 describes 'simple and understandable experiments to demonstrate the accuracy of EPIC-ATAC.' The validation on true bulk samples is explicitly accepted.

results.result: EPIC-ATAC was benchmarked against DeconPeaker, CIBERSORTx, quanTIseq, ABIS, and MCPcounter on PBMC datasets. Many tools showed similar high correlation and low RMSE values with no single tool consistently outperforming others, demonstrating broad applicability of the marker peaks and reference profiles across different deconvolution methods.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the benchmarking approach and results. Reviewer 2 acknowledges the comparison to 'deconvolution methods that were originally developed for transcriptomics' and notes the authors 'described in detail the specific settings used to analyze this different data modality as robustly as possible.' Reviewer 3 states the authors 'have been robust in their benchmarking endeavours and measured EPIC-ATAC against multiple datasets and tools.'

results.result: EPIC-ATAC accurately predicted proportions of both characterized cell types and uncharacterized cells (including cancer cells) in tumor samples from basal cell carcinoma, gynecological cancers, and HTAN datasets. EPIC-ATAC was the only method to accurately predict uncharacterized cell proportions, outperforming other tools including quanTIseq which also attempts this prediction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this key capability. Reviewer 1 notes the tool 'advances existing methods by utilizing a comprehensive reference profile for major cancer-relevant cell types,' implicitly accepting the uncharacterized cell prediction. Reviewer 2 states the tool 'successfully predicts accurate proportions of immune cells in bulk tumour samples,' and Reviewer 3 confirms 'EPIC-ATAC seems to perform well in benchmarking analyses.' The unique ability to predict uncharacterized cells is not questioned.

results.result: When applied to a breast cancer cohort of 42 samples (35 ER+/HER2- and 7 TNBC), EPIC-ATAC predictions showed high correlation (0.5-0.94) with the original study's infiltration metrics. EPIC-ATAC identified higher T, B, and NK cell proportions in TNBC vs ER+/HER2- samples and differences between ER+/HER2- subgroups, largely recapitulating findings from the original study while providing additional insights on NK cells and macrophages.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the breast cancer application. Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'the methodology and its application results on breast cancer tumor tissues are convincing.' Reviewer 2 notes the tool 'accurately quantifies their immune contexture' when applied to breast cancer. The comparison with the original study's findings and the additional insights are not questioned.

results.result: EPIC-ATAC showed variable accuracy across cell types, with lower correlation for low-abundant populations (NK cells, endothelial cells, neutrophils, dendritic cells). The average absolute error was 8% across cell types, consistent with RNA-Seq deconvolution. Low RMSE for endothelial/dendritic cells suggests reliable within-sample quantification despite lower between-sample precision. The authors note quantification of low-frequency populations remains challenging.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these limitations without critique. The acknowledgment of challenges with low-abundance cell types is treated as an honest assessment rather than a fundamental flaw. Reviewer 2 notes the work is 'of very high quality' despite these limitations, and Reviewer 3 states the tool 'seems to perform well' overall. The consistency with RNA-Seq deconvolution error rates provides context that reviewers implicitly accept.

results.result: When EPIC-ATAC was applied to T-cell subtypes (naive/non-naive CD8+, naive/helper-memory/regulatory CD4+), correlations decreased compared to using only CD4+/CD8+ categories, with particularly low accuracies for helper/memory CD4+ and naive subtypes. Similar results were obtained with other deconvolution tools, indicating a general limitation of reference-based methods for closely related cell types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this limitation without objection. The finding that closely related cell types are difficult to distinguish is treated as an expected limitation of the approach rather than a failure. The authors' recommendation to use major cell-type populations rather than subtypes is implicitly accepted as reasonable. No reviewer questions this aspect of the work.

results.result: Comparison of EPIC-ATAC with EPIC-RNA on multiome data showed similar performance between ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq modalities, with EPIC-ATAC outperforming gene activity-based deconvolution. On matched bulk PBMC samples, each modality performed better for different cell types (EPIC-ATAC better for CD8+, CD4+, NK; EPIC-RNA better for B cells, neutrophils, monocytes), and averaging predictions from both modalities showed moderate improvement, suggesting complementarity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the comparison between modalities without critique. The finding that ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq provide complementary information is treated as a valuable insight. Reviewer 2 notes the work demonstrates 'both modalities led to similar performances and that they could complement each other.' The comparison is viewed as strengthening rather than undermining the EPIC-ATAC approach.

results.result: Different deconvolution tools produce different output types: EPIC-ATAC and quanTIseq provide absolute cell-type fractions including uncharacterized cells, while CIBERSORTx/DeconPeaker provide relative fractions and ABIS/MCPcounter provide arbitrary scores. When benchmarking included uncharacterized cells, EPIC-ATAC and quanTIseq had a clear advantage. When excluding uncharacterized cells and rescaling, EPIC-ATAC still outperformed most other methods.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this methodological distinction and the two-part benchmarking approach. Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'described in detail the specific settings used to analyze this different data modality as robustly as possible, and they discussed possible limitations and ideas for future improvement.' The fair comparison approach is implicitly endorsed through the overall positive evaluation.

results.result: All benchmarked deconvolution tools require limited computational resources, running in less than 20 seconds on average.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the computational efficiency claims. This practical consideration is accepted without comment, likely because it demonstrates the tools are feasible for routine use. The lack of any concerns about computational requirements indicates implicit acceptance.

Both support cancer sample validation and uncharacterized cell prediction (C116-C123). OpenEval validates the methodology and interpretation with appropriate caveats, while peer reviewers affirm the tool 'successfully predicts accurate proportions' in tumor samples.

Both support benchmarking on cancer datasets showing EPIC-ATAC superiority (C124-C133). OpenEval validates performance metrics and methodological distinctions, while peer reviewers confirm 'EPIC-ATAC seems to perform well in benchmarking analyses.'

Both address the absolute vs. relative fraction distinction and two-benchmark approach (C127-C133). OpenEval validates this methodological consideration, while peer reviewers accept the 'detailed' description of settings for robust comparison.

Both support cell-type-specific performance analysis and acknowledge limitations for low-abundance cells (C135-C141, C199-C202). OpenEval provides detailed correlation/RMSE analysis, while peer reviewers treat these as honest assessments rather than fundamental flaws.

Both support T-cell subtype analysis and accept decreased performance for closely related subtypes (C142-C149). OpenEval validates the limitation with empirical evidence, while peer reviewers accept this as an expected limitation rather than a failure.

Both strongly support the breast cancer cohort application (C6, C150-C162). OpenEval validates correlation with original study metrics and additional findings, while peer reviewers explicitly state the 'application results on breast cancer tumor tissues are convincing.'

Both support the modality comparison analysis (C163-C171). OpenEval validates the methodology and performance comparison, while peer reviewers note the demonstration that 'both modalities led to similar performances and that they could complement each other.'

Both support matched bulk data analysis showing complementarity (C172-C178). OpenEval validates cell-type-specific differences and moderate improvement from averaging, while peer reviewers view this as strengthening the EPIC-ATAC approach.

Both support the uncharacterized cell prediction capability (C186, C188). OpenEval validates this as a key distinguishing feature with appropriate caveats, while peer reviewers affirm the tool 'advances existing methods' through comprehensive reference profiles.

Both support the honest assessment of accuracy and limitations (C199-C202). OpenEval validates the 8% average error as consistent with RNA-Seq methods, while peer reviewers accept these limitations as part of 'very high quality' work.

Both support the T-cell subtype limitation and recommendation (C203-C205). OpenEval validates this with empirical evidence, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the recommendation to use major cell-type populations as reasonable.

Both support the finding of similar performance between ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq modalities (C208). OpenEval validates this with pseudobulk and bulk PBMC analyses, while peer reviewers accept the complementarity finding.

Both support the main contributions summary (C220-C222). OpenEval validates these as accurate summaries of major findings, while peer reviewers affirm the overall quality and rigor of the methodology and results.
Peer reviewers accept computational efficiency (C134) without comment, indicating implicit acceptance. No corresponding detailed OpenEval assessment of computational requirements was found.
